title: Haunted Houses
author: H. W. Longfellow
tagline: Poem · reflective · the living and the dead share one world

sourceNote.thirdParty: "Haunted Houses" is a poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, first published in the nineteenth century and now in the public domain in most countries. Only one very short extract is quoted here; the rest of the poem is not reproduced. Read the full poem in your prescribed textbook.
sourceNote.boardprep: The paraphrase, notes on theme, tone and devices, vocabulary and all questions and answers on this page were written by BoardPrep as original study material and are not taken from any textbook or guide.

overview.intro: Most people picture a haunted house as a frightening place with a ghost in the cellar. Longfellow turns this idea around. For him every house in which people have lived and died is haunted, because those who lived there have left something of themselves behind. The ghosts are harmless and quiet, they move about their old homes without a sound, and they mingle gently with the living. The poem goes on to suggest that the world of the departed and the world of the living are not really separate, and that even our own minds are visited by memories and presences we cannot see.

learn.title: What the poem says, stage by stage

blocks.text: This is a broad paraphrase. Read the poem in your textbook and match each stage to the lines.

items: Stage 1 (the opening idea): the poet declares that every house in which people have lived and died is haunted. This is a general truth about all such houses, not just the spooky ones in stories.

Stage 2 (the ghosts at home): the spirits of the dead pass silently through the open doors of their old houses. They are harmless and seem to be going about small, familiar errands, and their feet make no noise on the floors.

Stage 3 (the meeting of two worlds): the departed and the living occupy the same rooms. The ghosts join the household at the table and by the fireside, though the living do not see them and may only feel a vague sense of company.

Stage 4 (the unseen all around): the poet widens the idea from houses to the whole world. The realm of the dead surrounds the ordinary world, close to us, so that there is no hard wall between what we can see and what we cannot.

Stage 5 (the inner haunting): the poem turns inward. Our own minds and hearts are also visited by shadows of the past, such as memories, dreams and feelings, that come and go like guests we did not invite.
Stage 6 (the closing thought): the poet ends with a quiet acceptance that the unseen world is a constant part of life, and that we are never entirely alone or apart from those who came before us.

blocks.text: The poem says that the dead are not entirely gone. They remain present in the homes they lived in and in the memories of the living, and the boundary between the visible and the invisible world is thin. The idea is comforting instead of frightening: to be haunted is simply to be connected with those who lived before us.
A second idea sits beside this: the human mind is itself a house with many rooms, visited by the spirits of thought, memory and feeling. We are haunted from within as well as from outside.

items: Tone: quiet, reflective and calm. The poet speaks as a thinker sharing an observation, not as a storyteller trying to scare.
Mood: gentle, mysterious and slightly wistful. The reader feels the closeness of the past and a soft sadness rather than fear.
The words used for the ghosts, such as harmless and silent, keep the mood peaceful and remove the usual terror of ghost stories.

items.meaning: The unseen world and the spirits are described as if they were people with habits: they glide about on errands, sit with the family and move through rooms. This makes the ghosts seem familiar and friendly.
The idea of 'harmless phantoms' contradicts our usual picture of ghosts as threatening. It makes the reader think again about what a haunting really means.
The human mind is treated as a haunted house of its own, a place where past thoughts and feelings return uninvited.
Images of open doors, silent feet, and a fireside gathering create a picture of a quiet, lived-in home, filled with the unseen.
A steady, unhurried rhythm and rhyme give the poem a calm, murmuring music that matches its peaceful subject.

items: Begin theme answers by saying what the poet means by 'haunted'. It is not fear but presence.
Mention both haunting of houses and haunting of the mind; many students only write about the first.
When you name a device, give one example and then say what effect it has on the reader.
Stress that the ghosts are gentle. Describing them as terrifying is the most common mistake.

keyPoints: The poet claims that every house where people have lived and died is haunted.
The ghosts are harmless and silent, and they go about their old homes like family members.
The living and the dead share one world, and there is no hard boundary between them.
The unseen world is all around us, and we are also haunted from within by memory and thought.
The tone is calm and reflective, not frightening.
examFocus: What does the poet mean by calling every house 'haunted'?
Why are the ghosts not frightening, and how does the poet make them seem gentle?
The idea that the living and the dead share one world.
The idea that the human mind is also haunted.
Devices: personification, paradox, metaphor and imagery.
Tone and mood of the poem.

questions.prompt: According to the poet, which houses are haunted?
options: Only old houses that have been left empty
Only houses where a crime has taken place
All houses in which people have lived and died
questions.answer: All houses in which people have lived and died.
questions.explanation: The poet begins with a general claim about every house where people have lived and died, not just the eerie ones of stories.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing empty or old houses. The poem is about all homes.

questions.prompt: What is the tone of 'Haunted Houses'?
questions.explanation: The poet treats ghosts as quiet, harmless presences, and the steady rhythm supports a peaceful mood.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that any poem about ghosts must be frightening.

questions.prompt: Which device is used when the poet describes the unseen spirits as moving about, gliding and sitting with a household like people?
questions.explanation: The spirits are given human habits, such as errands and company at the fireside, so they seem familiar rather than fearful.
questions.commonMistake: Naming hyperbole because the idea is unusual. Nothing is being exaggerated for effect.

questions.extract: All houses wherein men have lived and died / Are haunted houses.
questions.prompt: These words open the poem. Explain what the poet means by calling all such houses haunted, and say how this idea differs from the usual picture of a haunted house.
questions.answer: The poet means that every house where people have lived and died still carries some presence of those people, in memory and atmosphere, so no such house is truly empty of them. This differs from the usual picture, in which only a few gloomy, deserted houses are haunted by frightening ghosts. Here the idea is universal and gentle: to be haunted is to be connected with the people who lived before.
questions.explanation: Say what the poet claims, then contrast it with the ordinary idea of a haunted house.
questions.commonMistake: Explaining the line as a warning to be afraid.

questions.prompt: How does the poet describe the ghosts that move about the houses?
questions.answer: The ghosts are harmless and silent. They pass through the open doors and move about their old homes as though going about small errands, and their feet make no sound on the floors. They seem more like quiet members of the household than threatening spirits.
questions.explanation: Two marks: harmless and silent, plus the idea of familiar, everyday movement.
questions.commonMistake: Describing them as terrifying or cruel.

questions.prompt: In what way, according to the poem, do the living and the dead share the same world?
questions.answer: The poet imagines the spirits of the departed joining the living in the same rooms, at the table and by the fireside, though the living cannot see them. In this way the two groups are together in one home. The poem also widens the idea to say that the unseen world of the dead lies all around the visible world, so there is no firm wall between them.
questions.explanation: Mention the shared rooms and the wider idea of the unseen world all around us.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that the dead and living meet in dreams only. The poem describes a constant, quiet presence.

questions.prompt: How does Longfellow make an idea usually connected with fear seem comforting? Refer to the ghosts, the tone and the language of the poem.
questions.answer: Longfellow removes the usual terror by describing his ghosts as harmless and silent visitors who go about ordinary errands and sit with the family. This personification makes them seem like familiar people. His tone is calm and reflective, and the steady, murmuring rhythm keeps the mood peaceful. Words that suggest gentleness and quiet replace the shock and noise of ghost stories. As a result, the reader comes to feel that being haunted means being connected with those who came before us, and this is a source of comfort rather than dread.
questions.explanation: Cover three points: the picture of the ghosts, the tone, and the effect on the reader.
questions.commonMistake: Listing devices without explaining how they create the comforting effect.

questions.prompt: The poem moves from haunted houses to the haunting of the human mind. Explain this development and why it gives the poem depth.
questions.answer: The poem begins with a concrete picture of ghosts moving through the rooms of real houses. It then widens the idea to say that the unseen world surrounds the visible one, and finally turns inward, suggesting that the human mind is also visited by presences such as memories, dreams and feelings that come and go without invitation. This makes the mind a kind of haunted house too. The development gives the poem depth because it turns a simple ghost image into a reflection on the way the past lives on in us. What seemed a strange fancy becomes an accurate description of ordinary experience: we all carry those who came before us and moments we cannot forget.
questions.explanation: Show the movement in three steps (house, wider world, mind) and then explain the effect.
questions.commonMistake: Ignoring the last part of the poem and writing only about physical houses.

questions.prompt: Do you think the poet's idea that the departed remain present in the places they lived is a comforting one? Give reasons from the poem and from your own experience.
questions.answer: I find it comforting because it suggests that loss is not total. In the poem the ghosts are peaceful and remain part of the home, so the living are never entirely cut off from earlier generations. In real life a grandparent's chair, a house filled with old photographs, or a family recipe can bring a similar sense of company, and remembering them makes us feel less alone. However, the idea can also be sad, because the presence is unseen and cannot answer us, and some people may find it painful to be reminded of those they miss. The poet clearly chooses the gentler reading, and the poem's calm tone invites us to do the same.
questions.explanation: Any reasoned view is acceptable if it uses the poem and a personal or general example, and recognises the other side.
questions.commonMistake: Giving a personal opinion without reference to the poem.

questions.prompt: Identify two poetic devices used in 'Haunted Houses' and explain the effect of each.
questions.answer: Personification: the spirits are shown gliding about, going on errands and sitting with the household, which makes them seem like familiar people and takes away fear. Paradox: calling the phantoms harmless goes against the usual idea of ghosts, and it surprises the reader into seeing hauntings as gentle. Both devices support the calm, comforting mood of the poem.
questions.explanation: Name each device, give a specific example in your own words, and state its effect.
questions.commonMistake: Naming a device without any example or effect.
